questions.prompt: A patient's history lists prior uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP). Which description is most accurate for the technologist's documentation?
options: Prior upper-airway surgery involving the uvula/soft palate and pharyngeal tissues; current study findings must still be documented without assuming the OSA is resolved.
Prior maxillomandibular advancement that moved both jaws forward; no further respiratory monitoring is needed.
Implantation of a hypoglossal-nerve stimulator; the device should be programmed by the technologist without an order.
Nasal septal surgery only; obstructive events cannot recur afterward.
questions.answer: Prior upper-airway surgery involving the uvula/soft palate and pharyngeal tissues; current study findings must still be documented without assuming the OSA is resolved.
questions.rationale: UPPP is an upper-airway surgical procedure involving palatal/pharyngeal tissues. A prior procedure is clinically relevant history, but it does not establish current efficacy; the technologist should document present PSG findings.
questions.coachBobNote: Surgery names often tell you the anatomy.

questions.prompt: A patient using PAP for obstructive sleep apnea asks whether losing weight means the PAP can be stopped immediately. What is the technologist's best response?
options: Weight management may reduce OSA severity and can be part of the care plan, but prescribed PAP should continue until the treating provider reassesses the patient and directs any change.
Stop PAP as soon as weight loss begins because weight is the only cause of OSA.
Weight management has no role in OSA care and should never be discussed.
Reduce the PAP pressure independently as the patient's weight changes.
questions.answer: Weight management may reduce OSA severity and can be part of the care plan, but prescribed PAP should continue until the treating provider reassesses the patient and directs any change.
questions.rationale: Weight management can improve OSA-related outcomes in appropriate patients, but response varies and treatment changes require provider-directed reassessment. The technologist should not independently stop or alter PAP.
questions.coachBobNote: Adjunct means supportive; it does not replace ordered evaluation or PAP management during the study.

questions.prompt: A patient asks why a follow-up sleep study was ordered after a mandibular advancement device was fitted. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: Objective sleep testing can assess treatment efficacy and residual sleep-disordered breathing and can inform follow-up with the sleep physician and qualified dentist.
The study proves that the original diagnostic PSG was unnecessary.
Wearing the appliance automatically establishes that the OSA is controlled, so physiologic data are not needed.
The study replaces all future clinical and dental follow-up.
questions.answer: Objective sleep testing can assess treatment efficacy and residual sleep-disordered breathing and can inform follow-up with the sleep physician and qualified dentist.
questions.rationale: Symptoms and adherence reports alone may not establish physiologic efficacy. Follow-up sleep testing can assess residual events and treatment response, while ongoing physician and dental follow-up addresses symptoms, adherence, and adverse effects.
questions.coachBobNote: The question is not whether a device is worn; it is whether the airway is treated.
